runs.question: What two information security risks does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe, and how does NIST AI 100-2 describe indirect prompt injection?

answer.text:
The retrieved passages don't answer either part fully.

**Security risks in the NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1):** The two passages from this document are only front matter: a cover notice and publication details. NIST Trustworthy and Responsible AI NIST AI 600-1 Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile This publication is available free of charge from: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1. They name no risks. A passage from a different document, NIST AI 100-4, says that the profile highlights twelve different categories of risk from generative AI in more detail. It does not list those categories, so I can't name the two security risks from these passages. That same AI 100-4 passage describes synthetic content risks for cybersecurity and fraud, but it is not a description of the profile's content. In that passage, synthetic images, voices, or video may be used to fool biometric authentication systems or to mislead human recipients into facilitating fraudulent transactions (e.g., via voice cloning).

**Indirect prompt injection in NIST AI 100-2:** The retrieved pages show only that the term appears in the taxonomy's listing. It is catalogued as Indirect Prompt Injection (ID: NISTAML.015), and it appears under more than one grouping in that list. The passages give no definition or explanation of how the attack works. The taxonomy's structure is described in general terms: attacks are classified relative to: (i) the AI system type, (ii) the stage of the ML life cycle process in which the attack is mounted, (iii) the attacker's goals and objectives in terms of the system properties they seek to violate, (iv) the attacker's capabilities and access, and (v) the attacker's knowledge of the learning process and beyond. One reference in the bibliography is titled Data exfiltration from writer.com with indirect prompt injection, 2023., but a reference title doesn't describe the attack.

A different document, NIST SP 800-218A, does discuss injection in general terms, noting that user queries can be crafted to produce undesirable or objectionable output and — if not sanitized properly — can be leveraged for injection-style attacks. That passage doesn't mention indirect prompt injection and comes from outside AI 100-2.

To answer either part, the body text of NIST AI 600-1 (its risk section) and the section of AI 100-2 that defines prompt injection would need to be retrieved.
